conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martínez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived—something every new mother deserves. Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s a brief, 10-question screening that helps us understand mood and anxiety during the postpartum year; it also checks on any thoughts of self-harm so we can keep you safe. Everything you share stays confidential within your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you in the past seven days. I’ll ask each question conversationally; you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
Honestly… it’s been pretty difficult. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I half-smiled, but I couldn’t really laugh out loud. Things that used to crack me up just feel flat lately.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed. Even when my partner tries to be funny, it just feels kind of empty.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much anymore. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now it feels like I’m just dragging myself through the day. Sometimes I’ll plan something, like watching a show I used to love, but when the time comes I don’t even bother turning it on.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby spits up more than usual, I immediately think it’s because I ate something “wrong” or I’m not burping him right. When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., I kept replaying everything I’d done, convinced I’m just failing at this mom thing. Rationally I know babies just cry, but the voice in my head keeps saying I should be handling it better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep, nothing’s actually happening, but my chest feels tight like something awful is about to go wrong. I keep checking that he’s breathing, and even after I’ve checked three times I still feel this knot in my stomach that he might just stop.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits me out of nowhere—my heart starts racing, my hands get shaky, and this wave of “what if something terrible happens to him?” just crashes over me. There’s no real trigger; it feels like my body’s sounding an alarm for no reason at all.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… a lot of the time. I’ll look at the sink full of bottles and the laundry pile and just freeze, like I don’t even know where to start. Some mornings I think, “I can’t do today,” but I still push through because I have to. It’s like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Most nights. I finally get him down, but then my mind just keeps spinning—what if I’m doing everything wrong, what if he wakes up the second I close my eyes, what if I never feel like myself again? I’ll lie there for an hour or two, maybe drift off, then jolt awake at every tiny sound.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yes… pretty much every day this week. I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling I can’t shake. Even when the baby smiles at me, there’s this ache in my chest that won’t go away.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three or four times since last week. Yesterday it was because I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded—something so dumb, but I just stood in the hallway with tears streaming down while he started to fuss in the car seat.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

This new mother describes feeling emotionally flat, overwhelmed, and persistently sad since her baby arrived. She misses the joy she once found in small pleasures, feels intense guilt about everyday infant care, and experiences daily anxiety and panic-like episodes without clear triggers. Despite her evident love for her baby, she feels barely able to cope and cries easily.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to laugh or find humor, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for routine infant behaviors, indicating this happens "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intense, disproportionate worry (tight chest, repeated checking) that clearly maps to "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic symptoms (racing heart, shaking) and intrusive catastrophic thoughts without identifiable triggers, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm, freezing when facing tasks, and feeling unable to cope, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption due to persistent anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>The patient reports feeling sad or miserable "pretty much every day this week" plus persistent heavy, gray mood that persists even with baby's smiles, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports 3–4 crying episodes in a week, reflecting frequent emotional overwhelm consistent with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 26 meets the threshold for probable major depression (≥14). She endorses <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and <sym>sleep disruption</sym> most days over the past week, aligning with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Quote: <quote>I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling I can't shake</quote>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>PCP</med> or perinatal psychiatrist within 1 week for formal evaluation and treatment planning
2. Begin basic self-care: 20-minute outdoor walks, balanced meals, hydration; accept help with housework and night feeds
3. Practice 5-minute paced breathing when <sym>chest tightness</sym> or panic surge appears; consider free CBT-i or mindfulness apps compatible with infant schedules
4. Encourage partner or trusted adult to stay with baby so she can obtain 3-4 hour uninterrupted sleep block at least every other night
5. Provide 24-hour support line numbers (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) and local urgent mental-health services
6. Re-screen mood and safety (EPDS & Q10) at next pediatric or postpartum visit within 2 weeks; if <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym> emerge seek emergency care
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Post-partum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Demographic context: Postpartum mother, infant in home.

Screening tool: EPDS-style 10-item self-report (responses above).

Summary of endorsed symptoms:
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Recurrent, unprovoked anxiety (chest tightness, catastrophic worry about infant safety)  
- Panic-type episodes (racing heart, trembling)  
- Overwhelm / task paralysis with household duties  
- Initial and middle insomnia linked to rumination  
- No self-harm ideation (endorsed item #10 negatively)

Pattern: High endorsement of affective, anxiety, and functional items; low on pleasure/guilt; no safety red flag.

Screening significance:  
Score profile suggests elevated risk for Major Depressive Episode with comorbid anxiety features in the post-partum period. Recommends formal clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS scoring) and safety plan review at next contact.

End of screening note
